description: This open access article sets out a framework for deriving volcanic fragility and vulnerability functions for critical infrastructure and applies it to produce first tephra fall fragility functions for electricity, water supply, wastewater treatment and transport networks. Grant Wilson, Thomas Wilson, Natalia Deligne, Daniel Blake and Jim Cole of the University of Canterbury and GNS Science published it in the Journal of Applied Volcanology in September 2017. The framework covers input data from post-eruption impact assessments and laboratory tests, the choice of hazard intensity metrics such as tephra thickness and impact metrics such as damage or disruption states, function fitting, uncertainty and documentation, and it reviews earlier volcanic vulnerability studies. Coverage is general, drawing on impact data from eruptions worldwide. Format and access: functions given in the article's tables and figures. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: the authors call the functions a first attempt to be recalibrated as data grow, and they rest on sparse, mostly qualitative observations. They feed volcanic hazard exposure and resilience models of utility and transport networks. Related catalogue records are the Taal 2020 tephra building damage fragility curves and the Ambae 2017 to 2018 tephra damage survey.
